analysis: The closest response strengthens actual legal and contemporary institutional content by replacing an American-history research course with Transnational Business Law, persuasion with its required business foundation, and civil-society theory with AI/economic governance. Private/criminal/constitutional/rights/EU/international study remains substantial. No corporate-law doctrine is inferred from business functions or transnational transactions.

The public/international option replaces generic historical research and military-history content with criminal justice and ethics, and imperial history with policy analysis. Modern History remains a specific complement on state formation, nationalism, colonialism, war and international-order change. The commercial option replaces civil-society theory with criminal law, giving actual legal accountability greater weight alongside private/business law, finance and empirical business research. All three concepts remain evidenced, qualitatively distinct and above thirty credits each way.

Every selected course contribution was reconsidered using actual profiles or available descriptions, with full consideration of description-only public policy, econometrics, business strategy and market research. Programme-specific contributions are reassessed separately from unchanged shared description reviews. Material complementarities are explicit; rhetoric is not courtroom doctrine, financial markets are not insolvency law and modern history is not legal history.

All four initial offering conflicts are repaired. Actual earlier prerequisites and assigned offerings are checked directly. Introductory law/business/economics and statistics precede dependent legal/economic work. A preference for Microeconomics before Public Economics was tested and infeasible because Microeconomics requires earlier Research Methods and Public Economics has only its middle-Spring offering. Introductory economics and methods precede Public Economics; the additional order is not invented as a formal gate. The three schedules satisfy twenty-four unique courses, four per term, first-year PPD and at least six advanced courses.

Rebuilt all twenty-nine placements from actual content. Thirteen bounded relationships use important legal subjects or substantive methods: public international law is matched directly rather than paired with adjacent peace/conflict, substantive criminal law has the stronger primary criminal relationship, and transnational contracts match obligations. Negotiation corresponds to the instantiated mediation/negotiation practice pathway. Sixteen gaps preserve dedicated history, family/company/insolvency doctrine, empirical law/behaviour, legal sustainability, procedures, open choice and thesis. Rejected the old finance/insolvency, international-business/company-law and historical-paper/legal-thesis pairings. Optional research is outside scheduled credits.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.contribution: Academic writing, literature evaluation, civic collaboration and reflective practice provide the first-year common foundation.

BENBUSI112.name: Accounting & Corporate Finance
BENBUSI112.contribution: develops financial statements, accounting, organisational control, accountability and discounted-cash-flow appraisal, providing actual financial analysis for enterprise decisions

BENBUSI211.name: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
BENBUSI211.contribution: examines AI, firms, regulation, corporate responsibility, labour and inequality through business and country research, providing an institutional perspective on innovative-company governance

BENBUSI311.name: Transnational Business Law
BENBUSI311.contribution: examines legal frameworks for cross-border contracts, trade, finance, intellectual property and digital commerce, with advisory assignments and simulated arbitration

BENBUSI312.name: Money, Banking & Finance
BENBUSI312.contribution: examines financial instruments, valuation, banks, risk, regulation and monetary institutions, with bank simulation and evidence-based financial decisions; it complements corporate financing rather than teaching company-law doctrine

BENECON111.name: Introduction to Economics
BENECON111.contribution: introduces economic choice, markets, strategic interaction and government’s economic role as specific foundations for analysing regulation

BENECON212.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
BENECON212.contribution: examines incentives, uncertainty, strategic behaviour, markets and externalities as economic mechanisms that complement analysis of legal rules and regulation

BENECON311.name: Public Economics
BENECON311.contribution: examines public goods, taxation, spending, externalities and redistribution through policy models and research; this is an economic contribution rather than tax-law doctrine

BENECON312.name: Econometrics
BENECON312.contribution: develops causal and predictive economic-data analysis using regression estimators, tests and Monte Carlo simulation, with an empirical paper; this is a complementary analytical method rather than legal-doctrinal research

BENENTR212.name: Strategy & Digital Transformation
BENENTR212.contribution: examines business strategy and responsible digital transformation, providing a concrete organisational account of how technological change creates governance problems

BENENTR311.name: Market Research
BENENTR311.contribution: develops planning, collection, analysis and communication of market evidence, supporting empirical understanding of commercial decisions without claiming legal research methods

BENENTR312.name: International Business & Governance
BENENTR312.contribution: examines trade, institutions, policy conflict and cross-border business decisions, supporting the international commercial context of legal practice

BENGATE101.name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
BENGATE101.contribution: develops business models and the functions of enterprises, providing organisational context and the formal foundation for transnational business law without claiming company-law doctrine

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.contribution: develops empirical design, measurement, statistics and a data-collection project as a methodological complement to socio-legal inquiry

BENLEAD311.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
BENLEAD311.contribution: examines motivation, leadership, teams, power, conflict and organisational change, including evidence synthesis for organisational cases

BENLEAD312.name: Negotiation & Strategic Thinking
BENLEAD312.contribution: develops bargaining, interests, power, trust and strategic conflict management through negotiation simulations and scenario design

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice
GOSGATE102.contribution: introduces legal traditions, public/private law, justice and social context through case briefs, legal interpretation, mock trials and a socio-legal proposal

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.contribution: examines nationalism, imperialism, war, revolution, decolonisation and modern state/society transformations through historical evidence, supplying a specific historical dimension for public and international institutions

GOSLAWJ111.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
GOSLAWJ111.contribution: examines human-rights law, protection institutions, landmark cases and philosophical justifications through legal and normative argument

GOSLAWJ211.name: Criminal Law & Criminal Justice
GOSLAWJ211.contribution: examines criminal liability, punishment, criminalisation, excuses, offences and participation, with legal-advice memoranda and a criminology research proposal

GOSLAWJ212.name: Introduction to Public International Law
GOSLAWJ212.contribution: examines international legal sources, state responsibility, institutions, force, human rights and treaty politics through legal cases and critical research

GOSLAWJ213.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
GOSLAWJ213.contribution: compares constitutional structures, rights, courts and judicial review, with administrative participation, remedies and procedural fairness

GOSLAWJ311.name: Principles of Private Law
GOSLAWJ311.contribution: examines property, tort and contract rights across legal systems through legal briefs, comparative contract research and simulated mediation

GOSLAWJ312.name: Foundations of European Union Law
GOSLAWJ312.contribution: examines EU institutions, competences, legal effect, remedies, citizenship and free movement through current judgments and legal cases

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.contribution: develops ethical interpretation, normative argument and independent positions on moral theory and practical questions relevant to legal judgement

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.contribution: examines rights, authority, social order and political legitimacy through primary philosophical texts and normative argument, complementing jurisprudential questions

GOSPOLI112.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
GOSPOLI112.contribution: compares democracy, institutions, political actors and participation through empirical concepts, measurement and research, providing substantive political analysis of constitutional democracy

GOSPOLI212.name: Theory of International Relations
GOSPOLI212.contribution: examines state relations, international institutions, conflict and cooperation through theories and cases, with a UN simulation and researched negotiation

GOSPOLI311.name: European Union Politics
GOSPOLI311.contribution: examines EU integration, institutions, legislation, representation and legitimacy, with empirical parliamentary research that complements EU legal analysis

GOSPOLI312.name: Public Policy Analysis
GOSPOLI312.contribution: examines policymaking and analytical frameworks through a public-policy case and policy memos, complementing legal analysis of government decisions

GOSPOLI313.name: Peace & Conflict
GOSPOLI313.contribution: examines conflict, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice through interdisciplinary research and a policy brief

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.contribution: examines social institutions, inequality, identity and boundaries through social theory and evidence, complementing analysis of law’s social context

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.contribution: develops qualitative design, interviews, documentary inquiry, coding and interpretation for empirical investigation of social and institutional questions

GOSSOCI215.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
GOSSOCI215.contribution: examines environmental-justice movements, collective action and feminist/anticolonial perspectives through actual environmental cases

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.contribution: examines civil society, trust, public spheres, solidarity and social repair through theory and research on an organisation or movement, supporting the public-law option’s civil-society perspective

MCCCOMM111.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
MCCCOMM111.contribution: develops rhetorical analysis, argument construction, debating and public speaking; its communication contribution is distinguished from legal procedure

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication
MCCCOMM311.contribution: examines persuasion, framing, argumentation and ethics through research and community projects, supporting professional communication rather than supplying courtroom doctrine

alignment.rationale: Both examine AI, institutional change, governance and regulation. UCR studies business/economic and social implications; UvA develops legal analysis of digitalisation, platforms and government algorithms.

Both examine contractual obligations, risk allocation, performance and remedies through legal cases. UCR concentrates on transnational commercial transactions; UvA develops Dutch contract and liability doctrine.

Both develop negotiation, conflicting perspectives and structured dispute-resolution practice. UCR uses bargaining simulations; the chosen UvA pathway uses mediation and negotiation around a legal case with explicit reflection on professional roles.
Both develop the nature of law, legal sources, interpretation and case analysis within a social and normative framework.
Both examine fundamental-rights law, protection institutions and philosophical justifications. UvA integrates the operation of rights across Dutch and international legal fields.
Both examine criminal acts, causation, intent, guilt, offences, justifications, excuses and participation as substantive grounds and limits of criminal liability.
Both develop public international law through legal sources, institutions, state responsibility, force and contemporary legal cases. The relationship is substantive but partial.

Both examine state organisation, rights, government powers and constitutional constraints. UCR compares systems and includes administrative principles; UvA establishes Dutch constitutional and administrative law.
Both develop contract, tort and property concepts through legal problems. UCR compares legal systems; UvA establishes Dutch private-law foundations including their social context.
Both examine the EU legal order, institutions, national effects, citizenship, free movement and remedies.
Both develop reasoned ethical positions on conflicting obligations. UCR provides general ethical theory and practical argument; UvA applies professional codes and role-specific dilemmas for lawyers.

Both examine normative foundations of rights, authority and the liberal political/legal order. UvA additionally develops specific jurisprudential theories, legal positivism, natural law and legal interpretation.
Both substantively examine constitutional democracy, institutions, representation and threats to democratic order. UCR uses empirical comparison; UvA develops a legal constitutional-redesign project.
